utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that some preliminaries were to be expected. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Yes, we have been reminded recently by the Trial Chamber that there was an issue with Bill Haglund that was brought up in court on 24 July this year, where the Prosecution had offered to allow in or put in any cross-examination that the Defence felt they needed for Bill Haglund particularly in the Popovic case. The Defence has needed some time to review that, and it's our understanding in speaking with Mr. Lukic that they have decided not to use any cross-examination for Mr. Haglund -- any prior cross-examination for Mr. Haglund.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that Mr. Lukic is not jumping up and protesting so I take it that he agrees. That's hereby on the record. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And one other issue, we have a dead-line of 16 September for the bar table for Sarajevo documents. We've found recently we've been able to reduce some of those documents by reviewing the recent witnesses that have testified and the documents that have come in through them. We have a few more witnesses coming and we expect to be able to reduce some of the documents then too, but in order to get you the best product possible we would like to request a dead-line extension to 30 September so we can both explain those documents and yet reduce them to try to get them to the smallest number necessary for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We never object to any extension of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey, apparently there are a number of documents you know you'll skip already, others perhaps depending on what testimony will be heard in the weeks to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Wouldn't it then not be wise to already informally indicate which ones you would drop so that the Defence, Chamber staff would not have to bother about that at this very moment, but that would not be the definite list then but still others could be dropped as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll see where we are precisely with lists and what's dropped and get back -- get back soon with whatever help we can provide in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because that's how you introduced it, that you had decided already to -- that some would be dropped, would be skipped, and perhaps more to follow. So then the Chamber would like to hear from you, and perhaps also from the Defence, on ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But with this strong suggestion, the Chamber grants the request. Any other matter? Not from the Prosecution. Any further issue to be raised by the Defence? Not. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. I would like to use the time for the following: On the 28th of June, 2013, the Chamber, inter alia, admitted portions of prior testimony of Witness Music pursuant to Rule 92 bis. On the 1st of August, the Prosecution sent an informal communication requesting leave to add approximately 11 lines to the admitted portion. The lines in question are transcript pages 12.833, line 21 -- oh, yes, I apologise. I re-start. Page 12.832, line 21, until 12.833, line 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to know whether there's any objection by the Defence to that request. May I take it that you would need to look at it first and that we would hear, either later today or immediately after the weekend?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we would appreciate that opportunity since right now we're trying to figure out which -- which witness that is exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if you're ready to continue cross-examination, Mr. Ivetic, you're invited to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but of course I first --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, again we spent time on procedural issues and we were not very polite when you entered the courtroom. I would like to remind you again, as I did before, that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic will now continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We left off talking about intercepts and I'd like to return there. Now, during the course of this trial we had a witness RM279 who was knowledgeable about the ABiH's capabilities of intercepting the VRS and he conceded they could not follow VRS communications through the HVT1 system, the SMC1306B, or the FM200 system, and this can be found at transcript page 13.574 through 13.575. Sir, was such information made available to you at the time that you were making your assessments as to the technical capabilities of the ABiH side to intercept communications?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. It appears Mr. Ivetic would like Mr. Butler to know the identity of this person and if we could go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We could. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. What I was aware of was that they did not have the capability to collect on what was essentially data transmissions that were going over the various communication channels. They could only collect on voice communications. So again, without looking at what each specific piece of equipment that you've listed, the actual technical specifications are, I can't comment on that. But I did know generally that there were some military communications that was clearly beyond their capability at those sites to collect against.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did anyone at the OTP or yourself undertake to identify for each intercept that you were relying upon what particular type of radio relay device was said to be the source that was intercepted?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that many of the intercepts as written in the notebooks will have notations on that, but I did not go to that effort. I don't know if anyone else did or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, without identifying the locations, which I will refer to as just the northern and southern facilities, could you tell me if you were made aware of the locations of both, such that you were able to confirm the distance of those facilities from the communication relay hubs of the VRS that were used to transmit communications by the VRS in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that I visited back in I believe it would be either late 1998 or -- 1998, I'm pretty sure, one of the sites. I cannot tell you offhand if it was the northern or the southern site. I also know that we were provided maps of where the sites where, and of course not only from the documents that the ABiH sites were located, we also had corresponding -- at that time we also had the corresponding documents from the Zvornik Brigade. Many of those documents -- one of those documents that was particularly valuable was a copy of the Drina Corps communications plan, which actually laid out the VRS communications schematics and their locations as well. So again, you know, not necessarily getting it directly from the individuals at the site how far they were, we could certainly calculate how far they were from the various locations from the information that they provided as well as the information that we had seized as part of the search at Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now again returning to some of the testimony that RM279 gave, at transcript page 13.569 and onwards, he confirmed that for those radio relay devices used by the VRS which he claimed they could intercept, the manufacturer's longest optimal range at full power were 80 kilometres for the RRU-800 and 30 kilometres for the RRU-1. Did you have that type of information available to you and was it considered at the time of making your assessments as to the technical capabilities of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, not only did I have general information like that -- I mean, the reality is that, you know, I also -- I've given it some thought as to how I could actually explain this, so let me try it that way: As you're aware from my resume, from 1989 to 1992, I was an all-source intelligence technician in the 3rd Infantry Division. It is not classified, it's open source and you can find it on the internet, that at that time the 3rd Infantry Division had a rather robust capability to conduct tactical signals intelligence collection. We had what was known as the trail blazer system which allowed us to collect in the high-frequency range, the very high-frequency range, and ultra high frequencies. And we had the quick-fix system which was a helicopter-mounted version of the same equipment. Now, I won't say that I'm obviously an expert; however, I would suggest that for me to be able to do my job in the division with a robust intelligence and signals intelligence collection capability, I at least had to have a functional knowledge, not only -- you know, at least on signals intelligence collection. And again, it won't be a secret that in 1989 through 1992 our primary target of collection was the military forces of the former Soviet Union that were in East Germany who use a communications network remarkably like the one used in Bosnia by the VRS and in fairness remarkably like the systems that we used back then. As any radio enthusiast will understand, you know, the radio waves work the same way for everybody and consequently we all in the military structure our radio communications similarly. So at least, again, the inference I'd like to draw on this one is that while I'm not an expert, I certainly did have enough of a background that when I looked at this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, could I stop you because there may be some misunderstanding. Please correct me, Mr. Ivetic, when I'm wrong. It seems that Mr. Ivetic wants to know whether you verified on the basis of the documentation of the equipment used that the distances over which communication was intercepted was beyond what this documentation said would be the range of coverage of that equipment. Now Mr. Ivetic could have focused on that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree, sir, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- perhaps directly -- that's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and getting to that, because of this basis of knowledge that I have, I also understand that regardless of what the manufacturer says with respect of their radio range, you know, as a rule of thumb we understood from an intelligence collection perspective that we had an ability to collect radio waves out further ranges of that. There's a lot of factors that are involved with respect to radio wave propagation that intelligence people look at, you know, even amateur intelligence people like the ABiH back then, that go beyond the manufacturer's recommended specifications for the radio usage. So the distance to me doesn't matter more than other technical factors, like radiation power, condition of the antennas, and things of that nature would, to determine whether or not the radio equipment that was transmitting could be technically intercepted from a different location.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned the trail blazer device that could be placed on a helicopter. Do you know if the intercepts from the ABiH originated from aircraft radio interception devices of a similar nature?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, but again we put it on a helicopter to gain line of sight. The fact that they don't have a helicopter but they have a mountaintop essentially accomplishes the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in the course of your research, did you determine that the JNA had a training doctrine or protocol in place of powering down the radio relay devices from full power when covering a distance shorter than the maximum manufacturer's recommended range, precisely so as to keep or limit the ability of others to intercept those communications?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, and the same JNA radio protocols would have called also for them to place the radio receivers in locations where they would have terrain features blocking the radio propagation so it can't be collected by outside sites. However, you know, in a perfect world if you had enough equipment, I'm sure that the VRS would have really enjoyed the ability to place a radio communications network in the valleys where it would be completely secure for intercept, but since radio waves don't bend corners and they don't have enough equipment to do multiple stations, the option that they clearly chose was to use the few pieces of equipment they had, put them on high terrain, and use them to communicate. They took a risk that their communications could be intercepted, and the gain that they got was that they would actually be able to communicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a question at this point, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Butler, Mr. Ivetic used term "manufacturer's recommended range," and added to that "maximum manufacturer's recommended range." What is your understanding about this recommended range by the manufacturer? Is it a guaranteed minimal range or is it a maximum range in the understanding of the manufacturer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- when one -- in this particular sense, what they're referring to is the maximum range that the equipment will properly operate as the manufacturer intends it to operate. Essentially what they're saying is if you place the radio stations at ranges beyond these certain rates, obviously the -- not equipment is subject to failure, but the radio wave propagation will be such that maybe the signal's distorted, you won't be able to operate the equipment effectively. It doesn't mean that it can't be operated that way. It doesn't mean that it can't be modified, but again when you're talking about what the manufacturer's recommended range is, this is the range by which he guarantees, or the corporation that manufacture it guarantees, that this equipment will perform according to the specifications that the people who wanted the equipment built asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I propose now to look at a photograph with you. If we can have in e-court D00309. And, sir, I'd like to focus on the object in the middle, that looks like a tube attached to a plate in the middle of the photo. Can you -- first of all, can you tell me if this appears consistent with the antenna setup that you were shown when you toured one of the ABiH facilities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I'm assuming that there is a coil -- there's a Yagi antenna in here. I can't exactly tell what's inside the tube.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the dipole in the back, but I don't know if that's of consequence to what you're looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What I'm looking for is that in relation to this antenna, would you --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, if inside there's a Yagi configuration, it would be the standard antenna that one would use to intercept UHF range communications or to receive UHF range communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In this configuration can it receive duplex, or would a dual helicoidal antenna be required?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- again, you're just about -- at that point you're now starting to cross the line --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- between, you know, my functional knowledge of it and expert knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Understood. Now if we can look at D00311. And that is, I believe, another picture from one of the other antennas in this same cluster. Sir, I can tell you in relation to this antenna that RM279 testified that the ABiH 2nd Corps made homemade antennas from stop signs and toilet pipings such as this one. Would that information have been available to you when you analysed their capabilities, their technical capabilities of intercepting radio communications?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they did tell us that and I did know that, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now am I correct that as part of your March 1998 mission you interviewed an individual familiar with the VRS frequencies that said that the frequencies used did not change during the course of the war, which allowed the ABiH to fine-tune and intercept them easier?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that the individual frequencies may have changed, but the general radio bands that they were using did not. As you are aware from multi-channel communication, it's not one single radio frequency. It's a band of multiple frequencies that are in use. Some stations are transmitting and some stations are receiving, that's why you get what sounds like a telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And are you familiar with the explanation given to you by an individual that you interviewed in March 1998, that the VRS frequencies did not change?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we said. I take it that that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to look at 1D1243 and page 70 of the same in e-court. And if we could focus on line 8 through 15, sir. The question posed during the -- again, I believe it's the Popovic case reads as follows: "Q. Were you able to see the frequency plans of the VRS? "A. In the documents that we primarily use with respect to the Zvornik Brigade, which we had seized first, and to the Bratunac Brigade, I am not aware that there was a specific frequency plan with those documents. I don't know, having not gone through the entire Drina Corps material, the new stuff, whether or not there is a frequency plan for each of those networks in that, so the short version is: No, I have not seen a frequency plan for the radio relay." Is the answer as reflected here accurate -- accurate as to how you recall answering this question?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Even in the documents that we did have that outline the radio backbone, I don't recall that there were individual frequency plans for each channel of the network.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to now pull up 65 ter number 19848 in e-court, a Prosecution document. If we can zoom in on it so we can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have access to this type of document from the video communications schematic from the 1st Krajina Corps, I believe?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I've ever seen this document. Looking at the ERN number on it, given the ERN number, it appears that this is something that came into the OTP's possession after I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or at least was put in the ERN system and got a number after I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I put it to you that there's at least, I believe, one other document that I've seen of a similar nature. Would you permit the possibility that if such documentation came to the Prosecution after you left, that one could, as a preliminary step, look at the information contained therein and then go back and check with the purported intercepts to see if the -- if the frequencies match up and if all the other information matches up, so as to reach a new determination of the technical capabilities of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, it's not -- it was not my job at the time of the -- that I worked here for a variety of reasons to authenticate the network with respect to the intercepts for the Court. That was obviously something the intercept operators and those individuals who managed that collection apparatus work do. My understanding of the basis of a lot of these questions is -- relates to my -- the steps that I took in order to validate to myself at least the first foundational question of why I included the intercepts in my narrative and testified about them, which goes back to the question of whether or not the VRS telecommunications network as it existed in Eastern Bosnia in 1995, if it was subject to intercept and whether the ABiH had the technical capability to intercept it. That, of course, was the first step of my analysis and nothing at this point has been offered that would make me change that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, drawing on your experiences as an all-source intelligence officer, let me give you a hypothetical. If the frequencies that are recorded as having been used by a party do not match up to the frequencies recorded by those claiming to intercept them, would that reinforce or dissuade your skepticism in the reliability of the intercepts had you known that information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that it would be an indicator that the collection take that they were receiving could -- might not be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: By the way, did you consider the fact that if according to the ABiH they were capable of intercepting the radio signals of the VRS, that the ABiH would also be capable of interloping on the same VRS frequencies and broadcasting their own false transmissions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therein lies the difference between collection and electronic warfare. And as I suspect you are well aware, the power that you have to push down range in order to interfere or essentially insert yourself falsely into somebody else's communication network is far more than is required to actually collect radio signals. The radio equipment that I saw and that I'm aware the ABiH possessed at the time did not allow for the power wattage necessary to essentially bump the VRS's own signal X amount of kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree. But could they broadcast on the same frequency as the VRS within their own territory so that their own troops or own intercepted locations much closer could hear those on those frequencies and mistake them for VRS transmissions, intentionally or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. I mean, in the abstract that is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to look at one of the intercepts that you and Mr. McCloskey dealt with during direct examination, P12 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you have shown a diagram to the witness. I'm not -- first of all, there's no English translation for that in e-court. Now, I'm afraid that if you make an English translation you get the same undecipherable series of letters and numbers. I'm a bit lost about -- you don't want to -- the witness had never seen it before. I don't know what you want to do with it, what you want the Chamber to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, since the witness has not seen it before, I don't think I have a basis for putting it into evidence through the witness. We do believe we'll have some -- I do believe we have a translation now, if I'm reading correctly. But I believe we'll have a witness coming later who will be able to talk about this and the other documents, the other diagrams. I believe these are schematics of radio networks, but I don't want to be testifying and to have the Chamber rely upon what I say; I'd rather have you rely upon what a qualified witness says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, you asked questions about the document and what it would have allowed to do, et cetera, et cetera. So, to that extent to say that it was not used in any way is not accurate, but let us leave it as it is for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can look at P1235.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this was discussed by you on the 4th of September at transcript page 16.256.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We should not broadcast. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, looking at this intercept, it purports to be between General Mladic and an unidentified person, X. And you testified that this supported your position that General Mladic is talking about Potocari and that everyone needs to be evacuated whether they want to leave or not. Now, I propose to go through the B/C/S original with you. The word I want to focus on is located in the middle of the page and is spelled e-v-a-k-u-i-r-a-t c-c-e-m-o and it is pronounced "evakuirat ccemo," which is two words, and I submit is in the Croatian variant of the language. The Serbian word would be one word and would be e-v-a-k-u-i-s-a-c-c-e-m-o and would be "evakuisaccemo." Now, I understand that since you were working off the English translation this difference would not be apparent to you, but to a B/C/S speaker it is. General Mladic is purported to be using this word, the Croatian vernacular variant. Was this info known to you when assessing the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Again, I work off the English-language versions. I do not have any basis to be able to differentiate between an ethnic version of any of the B/C/S languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you find it odd, sir, that a VRS officer, indeed, General Mladic would be speaking in the Croatian vernacular?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's not something that I could comment on, whether he spoke it in the Croatian vernacular or whether or not the intercept operator who may, for all I know, be ethnic Croatian working with the ABiH wrote it that way. I mean, I can't comment on that one way or another. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did part of your analysis into the technical capability of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, has it a different meaning in the -- if it would be -- you spelled it how it would be in the Serbian. Would it have a different meaning or is it just that you want to draw attention to the fact that the way in which it is written down, that it's a Croatian version of the language which you would be surprised as being used by your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The latter, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The English translation of the words is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, did part of your analysis into the technical capabilities of the ABiH take into account that the ABiH used a significant number of amateur ham radio operators, as it did not have a sufficient number of trained professional signals corpsmen?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is what they told us and that is what we also observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can take a look at number 1D1079 together.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, sir, are you familiar with the FMSO, the foreign military studies office, within the -- as part of Fort Leavenworth, Kansas?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me the role or function of the FMSO within the US system?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are -- the Foreign Military Studies Office is an office of academics employed by the United States Army at Fort Leavenworth, which is where our combined arms academy is. Their job is to do in-depth studies of various military-related topics, many of them are military policy related, many of them are in-depth studies of what would be potential military adversaries and their tactics.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the lieutenant-colonel that is identified as the author of this piece?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to turn to page 7 of the document with you in e-court, where he has some observations as to events in the enclaves and the ham radio operators. If we could focus on footnote or end note I guess is number 4. And it reads as follows: "Rumours persist that the Bosnian Muslim government has hired some of these public relations firms to conduct media campaigns on their behalf in the US and Europe. Former President Carter was berated when he noted that the American public only knew one side of the story in Bosnia, but his statement stands as a concise and astute summary of content analysis available in the press. One of the best examples of Bosniak propaganda occurred during the battle for Gorazde in April 1994. The Bosnian Muslim government convinced the world that the BSA demolished the town and inflicted numerous civilian casualties ..." And then he lists a number of publications which I don't think I need to repeat. And then we continue: "The international media dutifully interviewed and subsequently printed accounts of refugees which government officials made available to them. Unfortunately, most of the media failed to corroborate these stories. The press also broadcast reports from a Bosnian Muslim ham radio operator whom they insisted had to be authentic due to the accuracy of his reports pertaining to the NATO bombings during the fight. Verification of these events later proved this reporting to be highly inaccurate, but the media had already moved on to further stories. Most of the damage that was done in the enclave had actually occurred almost two years prior to the battle when Muslims had conducted their own ethnic cleansing and burned out the Serbs' houses. As for the ham radio operator, no one who is holed up in a basement (as he claimed to be) can accurately describe events taking place on the battle-field. Rather, this person simply monitored the unsecured radio transmissions of UNPROFOR personnel who were controlling the NATO air strikes. He then mixed these elements of truth with his own propaganda to deceive the media. In fact, no conclusive evidence exists that the ham radio operator was even based in Gorazde." Was this incident or any other incidents of this nature known to you at the time that you performed your analysis of the reliability of the intercepts of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That question presumes that there's some sort of comparability between military operators on sites doing military work and a person in a basement in the Gorazde enclave. It's just so far away from the work that we're doing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- it has no relevance or value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. The witness may answer the question, whether you considered this incident or other similar incidents, if -- whether you consider -- first of all, were you aware of this incident? Were you aware of other incidents where ham radio operators were deceiving in their reports those who were supposed to read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of this incident and of course I've never seen this article before. In the broader sense - and again as I've testified before - obviously we were aware that the ABiH was a party to the conflict and would -- given what happened in Srebrenica, would have a vested interest to try and potentially steer the investigation or slant facts. That is why I said at the very beginning that -- by testimony that I looked at the material that was provided to us. You know, I was very suspicious of it, precisely because of an awareness that the ABiH was not a neutral party. They were an affected party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could move to 1D1243 in e-court, page 65 of the same, and which should correlate to transcript page 20.109. And if we could start at line 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And before I begin reading, sir, I'd like to advise you and the Court that 1D218 that is referenced in this transcript from the Popovic case is indeed the document known as 65 ter number 25575 in the Mladic case. And then I begin with the questions and answers: "Q. Thank you. Let us have a look now at 1D218. It is a letter of the State Security Service of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated the 24th of July, 1995. It is very brief. I am not sure whether this has been translated, although it had been requested. It is very brief. I'll read it out to you. "In it, a request was made of the 2nd Corps -- well, it reads: "'Given that in the latest offensive against the protected area of Srebrenica, the aggressor committed genocide over the Bosniak people. We kindly ask you that you require all phono material, audio material, pertaining to Srebrenica, from the assistant chief for security. The audio material is needed in order to open a file that will be put at the disposal of the International Tribunal in The Hague.'" If we can go to the next page: "My question is this: Did you ever see this document? "A. No, sir, I don't recall that I did. "Q. For you, as the expert, would this raise any doubts if even after such a request, the tapes with alleged conversations would be destroyed? "A. Yes, sir, I mean it would -- it would continue to, you know, be a piece of the weighting of information particularly with respect to my work on the intercepts, that, you know, would have continued to keep in the front of my mind that I always had to be aware of the material that I was working with that had been provided by these measures were a form of disinformation or deception, yes, sir. I had that in the front of my mind going in, and this piece of information would have just continued to pour weight on that." Sir, does this transcript selection accurately record your answers to these questions and are those answers truthful such that you would repeat the same today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours if we could tender 65 ter number 25575 at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We would like to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Let's call it up on the screen. 65 ter number 25575.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, just for purposes of connecting this testimony to the testimony that you gave in the Popovic case, looking at the document now, can I confirm that this was not a document that you had in your possession and that you considered at the time you reached your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I don't recall having this document in my possession at the time I made my initial analysis on the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document as the next available exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25575 receives number D359, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would but I think the interpreters would kill me if I tried to do a question in 30 seconds, so I suppose we should take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We certainly have to avoid that to happen, Mr. Ivetic. We'll take a break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can have in e-court number 1D1260. And if we can have page 3 of that 65 ter number. That should correlate to transcript page 20.123. And if we can focus on line 3 and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to re-visit the Popovic transcript at this stage: "Q. Let us go back to the first paragraph of the first page again. Did you notice that there, the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina state that all of the tapes they had in their possession, referring to the events, they forwarded to the Agency for Research and Documentation back in 1995? "A. Yes, sir, that's correct. And to further clarify, now that I've read this document in English, I can tell you that I have seen it at an earlier date, probably around 1997, 1998. So I can confirm now that I did have access and I did see this document at the early part of my work. "Q. My last question pertaining to this document is that: Did this raise any doubts, this fact that the AID has not been forwarding any tapes to you since 1995; although, they had them in their custody? "A. Yes, sir. In fact, this, among other information, was, in part, why I was prepared fully to not accept the broader body of intercepts at face value until the work of the OTP could independently corroborate them. This is just one of the many reasons." Sir, is your testimony accurately recorded and is the same truthful such that you would so testify again today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is. Again, in the context that we're discussing, I hope I've been abundantly clear about my initial skepticism about the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As an expert do you concede based upon some of the material that we've been going through the last hour or so that more investigation is required before placing undivided faith in the reliability and authenticity of the purported ABiH intercepts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that is exactly why I undertook an initial investigation before I included them in my reports in 1998 and 1999 and 2000. My position is that in 2013 I believe that their authenticity has been adequately proven and -- again, not to belabour an issue here, but the first part of my analysis was the technical issue. Obviously I looked at the intercepts from a broader analytical perspective and how they fit into the overall context of our awareness or my awareness specifically of what happened in July of 1995. Because, again as I've noted in response to both questions by all three parties here, deception was a possibility and I also understand the issue related to deception, you know, what it's meant to do at a point in time in the battle-field, just as the recent document the Defence brought up showed that this person may have operated and tried to deceive someone in 1994 and it was outed in 1995. You know, here you have a scenario where you get a body of information in 1997. One would think if this was a broad-scale deception operation, you know, from the period of 1997 to 2013, that would be evident. I believe that the opposite is true. I believe that when one looks at the military documents that were seized by the VRS that were clearly not in the possession of the ABiH and one uses that to lay out a context and that one looks at the body of the intercepts, it's not a technical term, but if you have a context here and the intercepts weave that context together, they synchronise. If it was a broad-scale deception operation, the reality as painted by the military documents on the one hand would run counter to the story being told by the intercepts. So the intercepts as a body of information are corroborated to a large degree by the military documents that were in the possession of the VRS. And when you look at specific vignettes like, for example, 17 July 1995, you will actually have intercepted references of military documents that were later found in VRS military headquarters buildings. The presumption I make obviously is not that an ABiH officer at some point deposited documents inside a secure VRS headquarters hoping that one day we would find that material. So again, when one looks at deception, the strength of a deception is highest at its initial point and degrades over time. We're now in 2013 which is, what, almost 16, 17 years after that initial deception was supposed to take place. I believe that's illogical.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you believe it's illogical that for every single one of the intercepts you went through the other day, the audio even though it was sought to be preserved does not exist, the audio recording?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That question was asked. We were told that they had a shortage of audiotapes for the systems. It was a reasonable answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know what percentage of the intercepts that you relied upon in your report do not have audio recordings in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time that I put together the report and the intercepts that I used, I don't believe any of them have audio recordings. I would certainly like to think that if we had an audio recording of that particular intercept, that we would have played it in court for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And yet for other intercepts by the ABiH from the same time-period, there do exist audio recordings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever seek out an explanation from the ABiH authorities why they withheld the audiotapes that they did turn over from the Office of the Prosecutor for nearly three years?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked that question on both the intercept notebooks as well as the audiotapes. Specifically with the question of the audiotapes, my understanding is the answer they had gotten back was that the audiotapes were forwarded to the military archive in Sarajevo. The war ended and they were essentially forgotten about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, not an unrealistic answer if you understand Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something else and whether it's realistic or not. Wouldn't also if someone has taken text of intercepts and fiddled with them, would it also not be realistic that they would get rid of the audio because that would reveal, as you said, the deception that was being played?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, whether -- for me, it's not simply a question of looking at a particular intercept in isolation and determining whether or not an audio does or does not exist. As I've indicated, there are other ways to corroborate the veracity of the intercept. One of them obviously is comparing the intercept and the information purported to be contained in it to the actual context of events that it's claiming to record.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree if one were to doctor-up the intercepts, get rid of the original audio, one would probably be good enough to make sure that it fit the context of events based upon information that was then known in 1998 that would not have been known in 1995, for instance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, the fact that in 1998 that the ABiH would have knowledge of 500 litres of fuel going to Colonel Popovic when the only document of that is a technical service rep? I mean, again, it's not that we did not explore -- I mean, personally I had to explore all of these alternative thesises simply because since General Krstic claimed that the entire body of intercepts were a deception or a montage, you know, that was my Rule 68 obligation at the time. And so, yes, I put on my intellectual blinders and I took myself down all of those rabbit holes, attempting to assemble information which would, in fact, support a conclusion that the body of intercepts was false or fake or had been planted. My conclusion is that that body of evidence does not exist simply because when you look at the intercepts in the broader context of the events that occurred, knowing what the ABiH would have or would not have known at the time because they did not have access to the VRS documents clearly -- and again, I didn't know at the time. Because until March of 1998, I didn't have access to the VRS documents or in April. So again, the probabilities that two separate bodies of information created by two separate armies pertaining to one contextual situation that occurred in July of 1995, and when you look at them and see how they correlate to each other I believe that gives me the basis to make a strong conclusion that the body of intercepts that I've used is authentic and purports to be exactly what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to switch gears and move to a topic closely related to the scrutiny of convoys and the distrust of UN and aid organisations by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can please have 1D1240 in e-court, and it should be page 1 of this document which is the transcript page 6671 from the Perisic proceedings. And if we can focus on line 15 and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, the questions and answers are as follows: "Q. We left each other last night having a brief conversation with regard to the Mujahedin. And I'd like to spend a few more moments talking about some of the contextual issues that involving around the time of July 1995. "You had mentioned in your testimony that, I believe, that there was also apart from the presence of the Mujahedin within the Muslim Bosnian army, there was also smuggling occurring that went through Tuzla. Correct? "A. Well, sir, the smuggling was the continuing effort to move manpower and supplies into particularly the eastern enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa in order to keep the 28th Infantry Division supplied. I don't know how that has to deal with the Mujahedin, insomuch as I'm not aware of any of them in those eastern enclaves. "Q. Very well. With regard to the issue of smuggling, were you aware of a meeting that occurred in 1994 in Tuzla with various members of the United States air force and Bosnian Muslim army members concerning supplying ammunition and other necessary equipment to the army? "A. No, sir. "Q. Okay. In the research that you did, did you come across any discussions about a secret airport or air strip that was being built in a place called Visiko? "A. No, sir." Do you stand by what is written here as accurately recording your truthful answers to these questions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I did not have that knowledge at the time. I still don't have specific knowledge of those issues. You know, my knowledge obviously based on the fact that, you know, the United Nations report does document it - I'm aware that they do - but I don't have first-hand knowledge of any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, now dealing specifically with Srebrenica and Zepa, did you have any indications of clandestine operations from France, United States or other NATO country operating in and around these enclaves in the time-period leading up to and including July 1995 as part of your research?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew, for example, that -- well, not clandestine. I knew that there was a group of I believe British military officers in the Srebrenica enclave, whose purpose it was to act as forward air controllers in order to guide in NATO aircraft during -- you know, at a point when bombing started on the 10th of July, 1995. That's the extent of my knowledge. I've always been very curious about the background voice speaking French but I haven't got to the end of that one either.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to look at something with you, the Prosecution document number 09930. This is a -- this is an UNPROFOR memorandum, I guess, circulating an article written in November 1995 by a person described as the ex-chief of the military information office of the UN in Zagreb who is, himself, a UN intelligence officer from Belgium, talking about his experiences in relation to the enclaves. The name of the individual is in the first paragraph, sir. First of all, are you familiar with either this document or the individual who is referenced [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could ask the Registrar to expand the -- I'm sorry, even though I'm wearing my glasses, my eyes are starting to go, expand the size a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Don't worry, sir, I'm also working off the hard copy because I can't see with my glasses either, so you're not the only one.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person you're talking about is this commandant Jan Segers?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Segers. Segers, yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of him. No, sir, I don't believe I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First enough. I would like to look at some of the points he raises. If we could have page 2 of the document in English and this will be page 4 of the Serbian and it's the fourth question on that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just inquire, does this reflect the whole of the article or is it excerpts of the article written? Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My understanding of it is that it is a translation of the article that would have been distributed by UNPROFOR at some point in time. I don't even know the date. It would have been after -- the article is written in November -- it would have been after 30 November 1995, but there's no date on it indicating when it would have been transmitted. The end -- the last page has the authors of the article listed which seems to indicate that it would be the entire -- the entirety of the article, but since we do not have the original text in French for this Prosecution document, I cannot make any affirmative representations on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could focus then on the fourth question from the top. I see it is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will read it to you so that hopefully the small text will be overcome. And this is how it goes: "How can you explain the so long survey of Bihac? "JS - thanks to the money that cams permanently, given by the Arab countries or by the refugees installed in Europe. Countless suitcases full of German marks arrived by helicopter or by road, brought in by locals or strangers. We even catch two colleagues UNMO doing this little traffic. They had 50.000 German marks and two mobitel, they have been send back on the spot. The 5th Corps sent for packages of money two times at night by helicopter. It is believed that the amounts of money who came in pro week were around 10 millions of mark, a billion Belgian franc each month." First of all, Mr. Butler, am I correct that Bihac was another safe area or enclave like Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, far north-western part of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we see here information about suitcases of cash being smuggled, including by UN staff that were caught and sent back. Did you come across such information in the course of your research and did you rely upon or exclude the same for purposes of reaching your -- for writing your reports and reaching your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came across numerous instances where the UN forces were engaged in extracurricular activities. Again, I testified even, with respect, closer to home with the Zepa enclave. Obviously there's VRS documents which talk about the fact that the Ukrainian peacekeepers there were selling fuel to the VRS. I suspect the UN was selling fuel to all three sides. It was certainly an issue that the VRS was concerned about, the fact that, you know, the opponents that they were facing, you know, could be getting illicit fuel and illicit support from UN sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3 in the English and page 6 in the Serbian, it is the end of the fourth question on the page in the English and it is the last line of page 6 in the B/C/S, going on to the next page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be some sound on the English channel which -- oh, it's the reconstruction work one of my colleagues tells me. Then we have to bear it as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll try perhaps speaking closer to the microphone, Your Honours, to try to minimise the interference.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, we are looking at, if I could just -- yes, it is the middle of the response of the individual to the question that is -- that is the one, two, three, fourth from the top, and his response in the middle reads as follows: "I was doubting if they were intercepting our messages, but one day I have the evidence. A Croatian colonel told me one day: 'Yesterday, in your sitrep this information was correct but this one was not.' When I asked him if he had access to our reports, he told me: 'Of course, yes.' Without knowing it or without willing to know it, the UN was working as a source of information for the Croats. This is unacceptable. I know that the Americans are given them information, but I think that the UN was doing an unpardonable mistake." Did you have such information that resulted from your research and was it considered by you that the US and perhaps others in the UN were leaking information to the Croats who at the time were allied with the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can definitely tell you that when I was putting together my reports, we had ample evidence that everybody was leaking to everybody. The UNPROFOR was a pretty equal-opportunity source of information for all three of the warring factions and all three of the warring factions did actively seek to collect information from it that they could use to their advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page, the top question, it will still be the same page in the B/C/S, although we need to scroll down to the bottom of that page in the B/C/S. And again, I'll read it so we don't have to strain our eyes: "Q. It has been said that there are military American advisers at the Croatian side. "JS - why not? It is clear that there are retired officers, Americans but also Germans, in direct support of the Croatian army. They are not representing their government, but they are there at official request. In Zagreb there is an office of 'consultancies,' a private company directed by American generals, which is given his services to the Croatian army. One day in Sector West, I requested to see the Croatian commander, a certain Djanko. They told me he was absent because he was visiting military installations in the United States. The same happened in Bosnia with the General Galvin, retired military chief of NATO, who was officially in charge as adviser of the Croat Muslims troops. Is this a violation of the weapon embargo of ex-Yugoslavia? I prefer not to pronounce me. One fact is clear, Croatia has bought modern weapons coming from the arsenals of the ex-Warsaw Pact countries. And to have this money, they should have been used money coming from drugs dealing." Did you have and consider such information that the US, unofficially through retired officers, helped both the -- both in Croatia and in Bosnia the opponents of the VRS to break the arms embargo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had that -- I mean, obviously I was aware of the issue with what was known as MPRI, a consultancy that did that. I was aware obviously from United Nations report about reports of US working with at least one side, the Bosnian Muslims, to violate the arms embargo. Obviously I knew all of this in my reports. I just don't know how it's germane to what happened in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me see if I can help you with that. With these things we've been talking about going on in the time-period leading up to July 1995, would they have given cause for the Serbs to pay particular attention to the convoys, irrespective if they were UNPROFOR or some other source, in your opinion and based upon your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and again as I've testified, you know, from the VRS's own documents, you know, setting aside these types of documents, the VRS believed that they had cause to want to ensure that equipment and material that could potentially be diverted for military use by the Bosnian Muslims in the enclave wasn't delivered.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would tender 65 ter number 09930, the document that's up on the screen, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I would -- Mr. President, I would like more foundation for this document. It is originally a Defence document. It's only got, like, four lines of purported UN type on it. It's not like anything I've ever seen. It's from an article allegedly and this should be independently findable from this Belgian newspaper. So if we could find out a bit more about where this came from and what it is before we let it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just to be clear, it's a document on the Prosecution's 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I take it that you must have an idea more about whether you'd -- 65 ter list means documents you consider to use as evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Not necessarily, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] well, that's what the 65 ter list is for, isn't it ?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Not completely, no. I think fundamentally, yes. But we put things on there to make sure they are visible available and we might have the opportunity to use them. They don't necessarily -- a document like this -- the fact that it is on the 65 ter list is certainly -- and I'm sure everyone would agree with me, does not mean it's authentic. The 65 ter list is designed as a notice issue, not as an authentication issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you would give notice that you may use a document which you consider not to be authentic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely, especially if the Defence brings it up and causes it to be authentic. It's not something that we would think about that's part of this case, but just because it's on the 65 ter list doesn't mean it's authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you would like to have more -- you mean even to demonstrate efforts of deception might need evidence which would then result in tendering not authentic documents, authentic only for the purposes of deception. Let's not at this moment try to -- one of my concerns - and I'm looking to both parties - is that some of the English is rather difficult to understand. Apparently the original is in French. Second, the document starts saying that it is an article by Mr. Segers and apparently it is an interview with Mr. Segers, so whether it reflects his own words is another issue that everyone will have to consider. I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will MFI the document and urges the parties to see whether the original French version is available; and if not, then to further explore the origin of this document as presented here. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 09930 receives number D360, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would now like to look at number 25915, which unfortunately is a document with no translation so I'll have to switch to B/C/S to briefly read the part of this order from 12 May 1995 from the Birac Brigade. So I give notice to the translators that I'll be switching languages and hopefully my pronunciation will be sufficient to allow it to be translated into English. I begin: [Interpretation] "Pursuant to available information, UNPROFOR members as well as of UNHCR and other international organisations are involved in illegal transport of fuel for the Muslims in the enclaves of Sarajevo, Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica. "They smuggled the fuel in reservoirs with double walls and larger reservoirs on combat and non-combat vehicles which are then emptied in the enclaves. What they leave in the reservoirs are smaller quantities of fuel which are enough only to enable them to travel from the enclaves to the territories of the SRJ and the RS."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [In English] Now, sir, have you had occasion -- have you had occasion to run across such documentation in the course of your inquiry into events in Srebrenica in 1995, even though it was -- would not have been available in an English translation apparently?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that I have seen English-language documents from the VRS which essentially say the same thing. Their concern was that basically the vehicles going in to the enclave with nearly full fuel tanks would leave with nearly empty fuel tanks and that was viewed by the VRS to be a potential means for fuel to be smuggled into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document has been used now I think with two witnesses. Can we get it MFI'd, and obviously it does need a translation but I don't want it to get lost in the mix of the trial record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number for the document would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25915 receives number D361, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. At this time I'd like to look at Exhibit D00141.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a situation report from the NorBat UNPROFOR which, it's my understanding, had among other places in Bosnia had some men based at Tuzla airfield. I think we can agree that the first page indicates this covers the period of 12 February 1995. Do you believe that you would have seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't discount that I wouldn't have come across it. It's -- I don't know why I would have considered it, you know, relevant to -- again, what the focus of my report is on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to page 2 and see if it does in your opinion. In the middle of the page within the "general overview" section there is a reference to the following: "Late Friday night an aircraft was observed flying at low altitude over the area east of Tuzla, with every indication that it was going to land. It was assumed that this would happen at Tuzla east where there is an extended highway strip. The UN APCs which were sent out to investigate the matter were prevented by the BiH (Bosnia-Herzegovina Army) from doing so. It therefore cannot be confirmed whether the aircraft actually landed or not or whether a load was dropped at low altitude ..." Sir, you earlier mentioned knowledge of some involvement between the US and the ABiH in terms of weapons shipments. Is this what you made reference to, that the weapons transfers were taking place at Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was making reference to was the UN's report on Srebrenica where they discuss that particular issue. I take it since this is a UN report, this is one of the sources they drew on to draw that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to look at D00140 with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you said the UN's report on Srebrenica where they discussed that particular issue, and you take it that since this is a UN report that this is one of the sources, although it says something about possibly having landed or a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I can say is, again, if one looks at the United Nations own report on Srebrenica, there is a discussion in that report - and I couldn't tell you exactly what paragraph it is - but certainly that report discusses and concludes the fact that there were clandestine arms shipments that came in from that area. Again, I take it this is one of the documents, but certainly not all they would have drawn a conclusion from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because it doesn't talk about weapons, at least from what I see at this moment, but in the context with other evidence it may be that this is indicative --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And again I have no -- I take it as a matter of fact I have no information that would dispute the UN's conclusion there and what I've learned obviously in the years since that is that in fact there is a body of evidence that supports this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can have -- pardon me, Exhibit D00140. I see it's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We can see from the first page that this is a letter from General Mladic to General Smith dated 14th February, 1995, two days after the document from NorBat that we just looked at. And if we can have the next page, please, I'd like to introduce -- talk with you about the letter to see if this was something you had access to. So please bear that in mind as I read the introductory part of this correspondence which reads as follows: "Dear General, "We are gravely concerned over the frequent use of Tuzla airport by the Muslim side. The aircrafts are bringing weapons, ammunition, and war materials for their needs. "Unfortunately, this pirate activity of their aircraft is enabled by the NATO airforce, and the Muslim army does not allow your forces to control the loads. "I am sure you share my opinion that these activities are seriously jeopardising the signed agreements and represent a serious breach of the truce and of relevant Security Council Resolutions. "I ask you to take urgent measures to stop these peace-threatening activities, otherwise we will be compelled to take the necessary measures regarding the Muslim side's violations of the Tuzla safe area, which is, in the presence of your forces, turning into a war base for Islamic countries." First of all, sir, do you believe that you had this letter and the information contained therein at your disposal when you were doing your research and reaching your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I've seen this letter, but again on the broader sense obviously I testified previously that I had a knowledge that during the conflict these types of things were occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There is a truce mentioned in this letter. Am I correct that there was a cessation of hostilities agreement in place at the beginning part of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the clandestine arms that were coming into Tuzla, what is your information? Were they -- was that their end point or were they being transported from Tuzla to some other location?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The information that -- and again, drawing from the United Nations' own report, those weapons, some of them were in part being smuggled into Srebrenica and subsequently to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could have D00142 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we'll see when it comes up that it is another letter, a protest, from General Mladic to UNPROFOR, this time to General de Lapresle. And let's look at the part that reads at the first introductory, two paragraphs that read as follows: "On 23 February 1995, at about 2010 hours, a transport plane, with weapons and military equipment, landed again at Tuzla airport's secondary runway. It was escorted by 2 NATO fighter aircraft which were protecting it during flight and off-loading. "Unfortunately, this has been repeated lately in front (within sight and hearing) of NATO and UNPROFOR forces both in the air and at Tuzla airport itself. Those forces are doing nothing to prevent the violation of the relevant UN Security Council Resolutions prohibiting the import of weapons and military equipment." Did you have information that NATO aircraft were involved in these clandestine shipments into Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I had specific information that it was NATO aircraft. But it was -- given the fact that NATO was policing the no-fly zone over Bosnia, I'm quite comfortable with the assumption that if they're not NATO-operated they're certainly operating with the knowledge of at least some NATO partners.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to 1D605 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for that, I can tell you, sir, this is a document that purports to be from the embassy of the Republic of BiH in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, could I have just a few small questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First, I noticed that the subject of this is expressed as, "Protest letter for General Mladic." I take it that it is protest letter from General Mladic if that is at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Actually, I believe if you read the explanation, sir, it indicates that it was signed for General Mladic on behalf of. I think "for" is meant on behalf of in the context of the note that says the signature is not General Mladic's. BSA HQ only advised us that it is the signature of another general authorised by ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The "for" then would stand for "signed on behalf of." I thought it was a letter, although signed on behalf of, but still coming from General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's one. Second, do I understand that well that this document is explained to have been signed by General Mladic although someone else signs for him without the usual "for" expressed in the document itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to the last page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- I really don't know. Unfortunately, this document is only in English, too, so I don't know whether it was written in English or whether there was ever a B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the -- this is the only thing we have, I see. I noticed on the previous document as well there was a signature there --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and which I don't know whether that was General Mladic's signature or whether the parties have any view on that or whether it was similarly signed by someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about the previous document, the previous letter of protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The previous document would have been 1 -- pardon me, D00140, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then have a look at that one in the original. Or was it the one before --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, last page. Yes, there we see something at the bottom written. Now, I don't know whether that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps if you can zoom in on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this -- how does the Chamber -- do the parties have any view and the witness have any view on how we should understand this handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no particular comment on it. I couldn't -- I don't know what that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's my understanding that this would have been a translation done by UNPROFOR so I don't know -- I mean, this is not obviously the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The originals are not available.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have to live with that for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I believe we were just about to look at 1D605 in e-court. This is from the embassy of the RBiH in Croatia and it's a list of a bunch of military supplies being sent to Bihac, again, one of the other safe areas, and is dated 29 May 1993. If we can turn to page 2 in the English and remain on page 1 in the original B/C/S, I think we will see it refers to the fact that these were sent via truck number UNHCR-10379. Did you come across documentation like this in your research about specific inventories of military equipment being smuggled via trucks that were marked as being official UNHCR convoys?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only -- again, I've -- not simply documents. I'm also aware of we have videotapes that were done by the Republika Srpska television company, RS TV station, you know, where the VRS is searching some vehicles that are reported to be either UNPROFOR or other NGOs and where they pull various weapons and ammunition out. Again, certainly it was an issue that the VRS was sensitive to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document, 1D605, as the next available exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
