utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D605 receives number D362, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just wondering, it comes to my mind that I've seen this document before. Was that another version or was it not admitted or tendered or ... ?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was used, I believe, with General Rupert Smith and at that time he did not have knowledge of it so I did not tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then, yes, then at least my recollection serves me well, but we now have it in evidence. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would, Your Honour. I think we are at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are at the time for the break. Thank you for reminding me. Mr. Butler, we would like to see you back in 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break. We resume at ten minutes past 12.00 and I would like to inform the parties that the Chamber would like to have ten minutes at the end of the next session to deliver a decision. We take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness will be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we can look together at 1D1246 in e-court, page 2 of the electronic version, that should correlate to transcript page 20.506 of the 28 January Popovic transcript from 2008. If we can focus on line 7 and the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, again, sir, follow along with me and I'll have some questions at the conclusion of this selection: "On the 15th of January, you mentioned the humanitarian convoys, and you said that your task was not to provide a comprehensive view on the policy regarding humanitarian convoys. I would like, however, to ask you whether you conducted an analysis concerning the period going from March to July 1995 regarding the number of convoys that were announced and the number of convoys that were refused access. "A. No, ma'am, I did not. "Q. Throughout the same period, you did not, did you, conduct an analysis about the number of convoys that were authorised access but that, for another reason, never went to the enclave? "A. That's correct, ma'am, I did not do that. "Q. On the 15th of January, you stated that the policy of the staff of the VRS, in terms of the convoys, was directly linked to directive number 7. Did you conduct an analysis of the policy of the Republika Srpska and its army regarding the convoys before the directive was passed; in other words, before March 1995? "A. No, ma'am, I did not. "Q. In that case, how can you say that the policy of the Army of the Republika Srpska, in relation to the convoys, was linked to directive number 7? How can you say that? "A. Well, ma'am, it's pretty self-evident in directive 7 what that policy is, so all I did at that juncture was then look at the convoy documents to determine whether or not there was evidence that such policies were being carried out. Now, with respect to the Dutch Battalion and their effect in January and February and March, prior to that, I believe their testimony doesn't reflect the fact that their soldiers were not being permitted back into the enclaves or that they were not being seriously degraded in their -- the supplies that they were getting until approximately the March 1995 time-frame. So, granted, while I did not take into account a statistical analysis of that, I did do it on a more anecdotal basis. "Q. Is it correct that you do not know whether the percentage [Realtime transcript read in error, 'personage'] of convoys that were refused after the directive was higher than before the directive? "'Percentage.' I was talking about percentage and I see in the transcript that the word 'personage' has been included. "A. Yes, ma'am, you're correct, I cannot give you a statistical break down." Sir, are your answers accurately recorded here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And are those answers truthful such that you would so testify today the same way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It remains the same today. I have not done a statistical analysis to determine the status of each and every convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can scroll down on this page to take up where we left off at line 20. "Q. Would you agree that the policy of Republika Srpska and the policy of its army was the result of the abuse made of the convoys because weapons had been transported in these convoys, as well as humanitarian aid for the ABiH? "A. Yes, ma'am. For the convoys, Bosnia-wide in general, the VRS was aware of situations where weapons and other illicit goods were being smuggled in on US -- UN vehicles, I should say, so certainly that is a consideration that the VRS would have taken into account. "Q. Do you know that the procedure regarding to the authorisation for humanitarian aid convoys was different from the procedure regarding UNPROFOR convoys? "A. Yes, ma'am, I believe that's correct. "Q. Are you aware that orders related to humanitarian aid convoys existed right at the beginning of the war and that the procedure did not change, was not modified, after the directive was passed? "A. I don't know that as a fact, so I'm just not familiar with convoy operations in the early war years, so I can't tell you 'yes' or 'no.'" Now, sir, is this select both accurately depicted and are the answers contained therein truthful to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, again when I talk about the issue of policy, it's the general policies related to inspection. I'm not meaning to imply - and I hope I didn't in this particular context - that 7 -- directive 7 where it talks about strangling the enclave, you know, is part of a broader policy of simply inspecting convoys to ensure fuel, ammunition, and weapons don't get into the hands of other warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the direct examination that you gave I may have missed something, but I don't remember you ever mentioning the existence of a co-ordinating body during this time-period that had certain authority over convoys. Am I right that such a co-ordinating body existed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, he's wrong that -- that was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. McCloskey, you'll certainly be willing to assist Mr. Ivetic in -- where he missed something. That happens to all of us now and then, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President. And my only point was that the question cannot inject an incorrect premise in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's why I say it was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not blaming you in any way for objecting to the question, but as a next step I'm inviting you to assist Mr. Ivetic to overcome his flaws in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which I [overlapping speakers] -- in the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we will listen and of course be supported in all ways we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I dared to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic was very careful putting his question: "I don't remember you ever mentioning the existence ..." And he added "I may have missed something ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, perhaps you leave this for a moment aside until you have found the source. I'm quite willing to assist you as well, if need be, and move on meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But the question was: " Am I right that such a co-ordinating body existed?" And this question can be answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, I think I recall talking about the fact that there is -- there was -- the Main Staff was directly responsible for approving the UNPROFOR convoys, and therefore other humanitarian good-related convoys I believe we did discuss that there was another co-ordinating body. Obviously the Main Staff was part of it but it was run by the civil side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In relation to that civil side, I'd like to look together at another transcript reference, 1D1426, transcript page 20.509 -- oops. One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel check if it's the correct number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Actually, I think I'm -- I can't verify that right now so I'll move on to another question, so as to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We think it may be 1246.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But still I'd rather move on and come back to it since I don't have the exact number in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 1246 is the one on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ah, I see. I apologise, it is the bottom of that page. We can go back to it then, focusing on line 10. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the discussion here is in relation to 5D605 in the Popovic case which is 1D01265 in our case. And the questions to answers read as follows: "Q. My question is the following: Would you agree that with respect to paragraphs 1 and 2 of this order, approvals regarding humanitarian convoys were issued by the co-ordinating body? "A. Yes, ma'am, they were the initial approval authority, but as you can tell from the remainder of the body of the order, the fact that they would initially approve a convoy, the Main Staff made it quite clear, in the body of the order, that if it wasn't co-ordinated through them, it still wasn't going through. "Q. But if you turn to paragraph 4 on this first page of the document, we can see that the document says sent by the VRS Main Staff to its subordinate units, was a notification, notification regarding the convoys that had been approved and the convoys that had not been approved? "A. What it's saying, at least to my reading, ma'am, is that they're complaining that one of the problems that they have is that even though convoys may have been approved by the co-ordinating body, they're aware that sometimes they're not getting notified and that these convoys are showing up unannounced at VRS check-points and it's causing a problem." If we can go to the -- yeah: "Q. I don't want to argue with you. At paragraph 3 on this same page, mention is made of the control of the VRS on the movement of convoys? "A. Yes, ma'am. It specifically states that the army has the obligation to check the teams and convoys passing through the territory." Sir, do you agree that this testimony is accurately depicted and that the underlying testimony by you is truthful?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would concur with respect to the fact that, you know, this is what I said in response to the questions related to the document. If you're asking for me is -- do I still have the exact same view of the document, I would ask you to put the document up so I can look at it. I would probably concur but I just wouldn't want to do so without looking at the document if that's what you're asking me to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can pull up 1D01265.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you can tell from the text of the transcript, it appears that I have a difference of opinion with Defence counsel on that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Please feel free to let the court staff to know if you need to go to a different page of the document. As I understand, it you looked at paragraphs 1 and 2 and then paragraph 4 of the first page and then paragraph 3 on the same page. So if the questions thus far related to the first page, but by all means if you need to turn to the others I'm not going to stand in your way. And perhaps while you're reading this, could you tell us if this would have been a document you recall having had an opportunity to review for purposes of the report that you did?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one? I -- as you will note from my earlier reports with the Srebrenica military narrative, I don't delve too deeply into the issue of convoy discussions because those weren't an area of legal concern during the Krstic and Blagojevic trials to the extent that they are now. I probably did deal with it more in the Main Staff report so, again, I did have access to those documents for that particular report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 2, please. Yes, sir. To get back to your original question. Yes, sir, I mean, the answers that I gave with respect to that time and how they reflect to this document are still valid. It essentially is an order by the Main Staff to its subordinates, noting the fact that even though they don't have control with respect to the approval of a humanitarian convoy by the co-ordinating body, if the co-ordinating body does not let the Main Staff know in a timely manner that these convoys may be coming through and what the cargo is, the Main Staff is telling them: We reserve the right to stop these convoys. Again, there's a war going on. The Main Staff has got to know about all these convoys, whether they're UNPROFOR or whether humanitarian, in order to be able to inspect them, check them out, and even, you know, in a more benign way to make sure that they're not walking into the middle of a fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to tender 1D01265, the document that is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1265 will be number D363, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could return to 1D1246 and it should be, I believe, page 7 of that document which should correlate to transcript page 20.510 of the underlying Popovic transcript. And if we focus on line 8 onward.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is -- it's in relation to the same order we just went through: "Q. At point 1 of this order, convoys that had not been announced were not allowed to go through? "A. Yes, ma'am, it's what it's saying, is that unless they receive -- unless the subordinate formations receive authorisation in writing from the Main Staff, they're not to permit the convoy to pass. "Q. In the remaining parts of this order, we have a list of the controls that subordinated formations or units are supposed to conduct when a convoy appears? "A. Yes, ma'am. "Q. Would you agree that these measures are precisely the same as the one that existed in 1995, provided of course you know what measures were to be followed in 1995? "A. Well, yes, ma'am, with respect to the technical goods and humanitarian aid issues, it just seems to be the same type of order. The fact that they're not to allow anything more that pass -- that's been authorised to pass, anything else will be confiscated, so in that sense it's correct. This order obviously does not regulate anything with respect to the issue of UN or even international personnel who leave a particular area and what the policy is on allowing them to return. So in that respect it is different." And is this accurately and truthfully reflected in the testimony on these answers -- on these questions, I should say?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with respect to humanitarian convoys there were several agreements that were entered into and concluded between the UNPROFOR and the VRS as to those convoys? Are you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that I'm specifically aware at the moment of the various agreements pertaining convoy regulation between UNPROFOR and VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I understand your answer. Would I be correct that in drafting your reports, in particular your Main Staff report, reaching your opinions you did not have any specific knowledge about the technical details of these agreements that existed between UNPROFOR and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I may have at the time. I just -- I don't recall them at the moment now. If I did, I would like to believe that I would have referenced them in the report, but I just -- I don't recall having knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could turn to 1D1246, page 7, and line 10 through 20. I think I can refresh your recollection: "Q. Have you had the opportunity to see the agreements passed between the VRS and UNPROFOR? "A. For which particular time-frame, ma'am? "Q. 1995, and especially after the directive was passed. "A. No, ma'am. I don't believe I've seen any agreements or any of the technical agreements with the UN with respect to those convoys for post March 1995. "Q. But before March 1995? "A. I believe my association with those documents relates to convoys passing between the VRS positions around Sarajevo. They're not directly related to Srebrenica." Does that assist you, sir, to refresh your recollection as to if you would have had the technical details of these agreements in mind when you reached your conclusions and drafted your various written reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least -- again, I don't remember obviously - and I'm consistent in at least not remembering - seeing anything post 1995 with Srebrenica. Again, it may very well be that I have seen some of the technical agreement documents with Sarajevo that related to an earlier period. I certainly don't discount that I did; and again, if I did so, hopefully it's marked in my Main Staff report or at least talked about in my direct testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can please turn to page 9 of this transcript, focus on line 4 through 19: "MS. FAUVEAU: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 5D727. It's in English. Could we see the signature at the bottom of the document. It's a letter sent by General Ratko Mladic to General Bernard Janvier. If you turn to the text itself of the document, you'll see that reference is made to an agreement passed on the 4th of June, 1995. "Q. Have you had the opportunity to see this agreement of 4th of June, 1995? "A. I do not believe so, ma'am. "Q. This document mentions contacts between the liaison officers in the enclaves with the local commanders of UNPROFOR. Have you had access to the material related to these contacts that apparently took place on the 6th of June, 1995, if we are to believe this document? "A. No, ma'am. With respect to Srebrenica, and Zepa, for that matter, I am not aware of any meeting notes or things of that nature that -- that would have occurred on 6 June 1995. It certainly may very well have happened, but I don't recall coming across any notes reflecting that." Does this accurately comport to your recollection of the testimony and is said testimony truthful to the best of your knowledge and information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, given it's a conversation between myself and Ms. Fauveau disputing or at least looking at a particular document, may I please see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This one I don't have access to in our system or at least I have not yet pinned down which one it is. All right. Well, let me ask you this: For purpose of your research and reaching conclusions in relation to the objectives of -- of the Serbs and the issue of humanitarian convoys post March 1995, would you agree that the existence or non-existence of contacts between the VRS and UNPROFOR and agreements that may or may not have been reached would be germane to your review or the type of review you were doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- I'm sure he meant Bosnian Serbs, but I don't want the record to reflect that Mr. Butler is referring to all Serbs in his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I meant Bosnian Serbs or VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the question moves from very concrete to hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Abstract in a hurry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I think for the Chamber to be fully able to appreciate the evidence, we'd like to have a look at the document itself as well and perhaps you may --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think Mr. McCloskey --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see Mr. McCloskey is so assisting today perhaps in this respect as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Stewart has found it as 17520 in our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While you're reading this, sir, perhaps keep in mind my first question will be: Were you aware of this document or did you come across it in your research.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I was aware of it, I don't know what I would make of it. I've read the paragraph three times, at least the first paragraph, and I don't know that I can make any sense out of what General Mladic is offering here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's try to simplify. It does reference the existence of an agreement entered into in June of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everyone who can read can answer that question. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have knowledge of any such agreements entered into in June of 1995, relating specifically to Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde, and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.text: Could I ask both parties: Is there any document which contains such an agreement because the line of questioning is very much you should have considered that agreement. I wonder whether there's any source which gives us the text of that agreement. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, as Your Honours have seen, I did not even have access to this document at the time that [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.text: Then, Mr. McCloskey, do you have a 4th of June agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of. But as you know, you can look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps I should have asked Ms. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I take -- no, I won't take too much offence to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could trace any text of such an agreement, then we would know what we are talking about. If you want to take instructions in this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. But you know at short, low volume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can assist, I'm told there may not be a written document from this encounter, but there may be a recording, a video of the meeting. We will investigate further and get back to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That saves such a lot of time, and this one as well. Go to the core of your -- of the issue right away. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you agree with me that for purposes of your review you did not do an extensive review of Ministry of the Interior documents to determine what role the MUP or the Ministry of the Interior of the Republika Srpska would have had in relation to authorisation of convoys of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I would conclude that the MUP's participation with respect to the humanitarian aid would be as a result of whatever participation they took in the civilian co-ordinating body issue. Again, my focus when looking at the convoy documents was the practical application of those convoys being able to move and under what circumstances. And ultimately, again as we've talked about in a previous document, it was the army that -- whether they had a vote at the co-ordinating committee level or not -- or co-ordinating body or not, the fact is it was the army that controlled the roads in Eastern Bosnia or in access to Sarajevo. And they ultimately decided which convoys passed and under what circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the MUP, I'd like to re-visit an issue from direct examination. At transcript page 16.405, Mr. McCloskey asked you and -- about -- at lines 7 through 15 the question was in relation to a Mr. Karisik that you identified as being the head of the RDB, the Republika Srpska State Security Service. In that relation I'd like to call up document 1D01259. This is a dispatch dated 27 July 1995. In B/C/S the header at the top reads: "MUP RS - RJB Bijeljina. [Interpretation] "Broj: RJB-314/95." [In English] And I believe we can see at the bottom of the screen that it is signed by the [Interpretation] Head of the RJB, Milenko Karisik. [In English] Sir, is this the same person that you were testifying about that you indicated was the head of the RDB or the Republika Srpska State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Looking at the date of the document, are you -- does it refresh your recollection that in fact he was head of public security at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may well be the case that I'm misremembered it. My recollection that he was head of the state security branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I wanted to ask you, sir, one of the check-points near Srebrenica known as the "Yellow Bridge," are you familiar with such a feature or a location?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this check-point existed from 1993 onwards at this location, and thus could not have been said to be established subsequent to directive number 7?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The facility known or the check-point known as the Yellow Bridge was the long-established check-point which was where you entered the UN -- you know, you cross the bridge and you enter essentially the safe area of Srebrenica. So yes, the establishment of a check-point at the Yellow Bridge was not a direct correlation to directive 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And specifically in relation to the Zvornik Brigade, I believe for purposes of your report you may have cited to two reports relating to items confiscated from convoys. Am I correct, you did not do a comprehensive review of the Zvornik Brigade documents in relation to locating all of them that dealt with convoys?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Again, with respect to the Zvornik Brigade documents and particularly my early work, I did not go back and look at all Zvornik Brigade documents as they might relate to convoys through 1994 and 1995, particularly up to March of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to the convoys, would you agree with me that there was a requirement for the convoys to have an inventory listing the goods being transported, both in terms of what they were and their quantity?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in your opinion was such a provision entirely reasonable, given the circumstances of the war and the acts of misuse of convoys that we've discussed here today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have said about that issue is this: Certainly the VRS from a military perspective had a right to inspect the convoys to ensure that goods that they considered to be military in nature or that might be diverted for military use would be, you know, either kept to a minimum because they were -- belonged to the UN or they were denied access in the enclaves. The question as to whether restricting the amount of broader humanitarian goods and under what circumstances that activity was reasonable is a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to call up 19596 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think you will see when it comes up this is a 1st Zvornik Brigade command regular report to the Drina Corps dated April 4, 1995. If we could turn to the third page in the English, the -- I believe it should be the last page in the B/C/S. Item number 10, sir, talks about the crossing of various convoys. We see two UNHCR convoys and three MSF, or Doctors Without Borders, Medecins Sans Frontieres, convoys that went through. And apparently there was only one that was stopped that material was seized and that's identified here at the bottom of this page and the top of the next page. And it would appear -- at least there's no indication that other material was not allowed to pass through. Would you agree that for purposes of your research where items were not on inventory, only the items that were not on inventory were confiscated and the convoys were allowed to proceed with all other items?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that that's the case. Again, they're in this particular document, it is an assumption that can be made, but again it doesn't specifically -- if I remember this document correctly because I've talked about it, this document does not specifically note the fact that these items were seized because they were not inventory items. They're noting that they were seized, no explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could tender this document as the next available exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I think it's in evidence already as P2157.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. And Your Honours said you needed ten minutes at the end of the session. I believe we are just about there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are close to that moment, yes. Mr. Butler, your break will be a little bit longer than ours. We would like to see you back in 25 to 30 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I would deliver an oral decision which is an oral decision on the Prosecution's motion for leave to amend its Rule 65 ter witness list. On the 26th of June of this year, the Prosecution filed a motion for leave to amend its Rule 65 ter witness list, seeking the addition of Witnesses RM096, RM097, RM098, RM099, RM182, RM378, and RM379. The Prosecution submits that these additions should be considered in light of its 20th June 2013 notice of its intention to reduce the evidence it adduces in support of its case. The Prosecution states that the decrease in both the total number of witnesses and live witnesses resulting from its notice and from the motion constitutes good cause for adding the witnesses to its Rule 65 ter witness list, as the Defence will require less preparation time for the remaining Prosecution witnesses and will not be prejudiced. Further, the Prosecution submits that witnesses' evidence either addresses issues and potential defences raised during the trial or addresses with greater specificity issues related to the Prosecution's burden of proof. The Prosecution submits that even if it lacks good cause, the witnesses' evidence is relevant and probative and it is in the interests of justice to grant the proposed additions. After being granted an additional 14 days in which to respond, on the 23rd of July, the Defence filed its response, objecting to the motion in part. It requests that the addition of Witness RM099 be denied and objects only to the proposed mode of testimony of Witnesses RM096, RM098, and RM378. The Defence does not object to the addition of Witnesses RM097, RM182, and RM379. On the 30th of July, the Prosecution filed a request for leave to reply, with its reply attached. The Chamber grants the Prosecution's request and considers the reply to be validly filed on the 30th of July, 2013. In its reply, the Prosecution submits that the Defence's objection to Witness RM099 was based on a mistaken premise, that the witness had not previously testified before the Tribunal. The Prosecution states that the witness has, in fact, testified in two previous cases before the Tribunal and that these testimonies were disclosed to the Defence on the 3rd of July, 2013, before the response was filed. The Chamber recalls and refers to the applicable law concerning amendments to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter witness list, as set out in its previous decision filed on the 22nd of August of this year. At the outset, the Chamber notes that the Defence's objections regarding the mode of testimony through which the witness will eventually testify are premature and misplaced. Instead, the proper forum for such arguments would be in response to a motion tendering the evidence. Accordingly, those parts of the response dealing with the proposed mode of testimony will not be further considered in this decision. The Chamber further notes that the Defence has not objected to the addition of Witness RM096, RM097, and RM098, and Witness RM182, RM378, and RM379 to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter witness list. The Chamber finds that it's in the interests of justice to add the aforementioned witnesses to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter witness list. With regard to Witness RM099, whilst the Chamber considers that the Prosecution has not shown good cause for adding this witness to its Rule 65 ter witness list at this stage of the proceedings, the Chamber considers the witness's evidence to be prima facie relevant and of probative value. The Chamber finds that the addition of this witness will result in a limited additional burden for the Defence given that the witness will provide crime base evidence on Banja Luka and ARK topics, upon which the Chamber has already heard evidence. The Chamber reminds the Defence that it has 14 days to respond to the Prosecution's Rule 92 quater motion relating to Witness RM099, a request that was granted by the Chamber on the 19th of August of this year. Should the Defence require additional time to respond to the motion, the Chamber will consider such a request. In light of the aforementioned, the Chamber finds that it is in the interests of justice to allow the addition of the witnesses to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter witness list. Further, the Chamber grants the Prosecution's request to exceed the word limit in the motion. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. We take a break and we resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness will be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, there are a few requests for extensions of time pending. Mr. McCloskey, is there any objection to any of the requests?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

The Defence motion to enlarge time to respond to the Prosecution's second UN bar table motion is partially granted and the new dead-line is set at 11th of October, which means 30 days for the Defence from today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And finally the Defence motion to enlarge time to respond to the Prosecution's 35th motion to admit evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis, that is about Witness RM275, the Defence had asked for 30 days. 21 days are granted, so you have until the 3rd of October, Mr. Lukic. If Mr. Ivetic is ready, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm ready to proceed. I would ask that we call up exhibit -- document 1D01269 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We had left off by looking at a Zvornik Brigade report to the Drina Corps about the convoy from Doctors Without Borders. We now have a report from the Drina Corps to the Main Staff from the same time-period, and if you could look at item number 3 I think we'll see that it says in relation to the UNPROFOR convoys and teams: "The situation is under control and all the planned UNPROFOR convoys and teams crossed our territory without any holdups." Did you do any research to determine if, in fact, incidents at -- in relation to goods being confiscated if they were accurately reported upwards towards the Main Staff or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, not in the sense that you're talking about, if I sought to do that. With respect to what the brigades were reporting related to that and then through the corps and then to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 1D01269.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01269 receives number D364, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections, D364 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would then call up 1D266 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is a one-page report from the command of the 1st Bratunac Brigade signed by a Captain Momir Nikolic and it gives some information. I'd like to focus on the last two paragraphs which state: "I would like to inform you that the co-ordinator of the MFS/?MSF/ - Medecins Sans Frontieres organisation publicly apologised for the abuse of /trust of/ and /one of/ his members in Srebrenica and publicly admitted that the Serbian side had behaved perfectly, correctly when it confiscated the vehicle and smuggled goods. This delegate - Jean - was removed from the MFS/?MSF/ organisation and returned to his country because of abuse /of trust/ and smuggling with Muslims from Srebrenica and Naser Oric. "The MFS/?MSF/ co-ordinator asked me to put this case behind us and said that it should not affect the further co-operation between the Serbian side and the above-mentioned humanitarian organisation." Now, did you have access to and review this report for purposes of reaching the conclusions that you did testify about in relation to humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you go back up first on this document so that I could look at the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. If you go in the original I think that would be --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a relatively low ERN number, so I gather at some juncture I may have had access to it. I don't know whether I've seen it offhand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have an independent recollection of this event, where the Doctors Without Borders made a --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, and that's why I wanted to read the whole document to see if it could refresh my memory as to whether I've seen this document or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you give me a minute, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I have not seen this document before; or if I did, it didn't stick in memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this as the next available Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01266 receives number D365, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D365 is admitted into evidence. Could I ask the parties whether there's any further information available about incident of smuggling prior to the 11th of January so that we know more or less what the seriousness of the issue was. Is there any -- could the parties see whether they can find anything on that so --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Definitely, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as to better enable the Chamber to understand the importance of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course I refer to 11th of January, 1995, which is the date of this document which was admitted a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I go back to the question Mr. Ivetic put to the witness last. It was: "Do you have an independent recollection of this event?" This is a question which was not answered by you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. No, I do not. I have no recollection of that event whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or I should say I have no knowledge of that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to document -- 65 ter number 1D01270.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is a code restricted report on the implementation of the cessation of hostilities agreement during March 1995. If we could turn to page 4 of the same, I believe that there is a section on humanitarian aid at paragraph 7. If we could zoom in on that and talks about the proportion of aid that actually got into the enclaves during the time-period, and it says the penultimate conclusion or end, I should say: "Approximately 18.000 metric tons of aid were delivered in total, compared to the monthly target of 22.800 metric tons. This success ratio breaks down as follows: "Bihac - 29 per cent. "Sarajevo - 71 per cent. "Srebrenica - 93 per cent. "Zepa - 80 per cent. "Gorazde - 83 per cent." Now, sir, did you have access to this document or access to this type of information independent of this document at the time that you were performing your review and making your conclusions as to humanitarian aid convoys in the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I've ever seen this document before. Again, this -- I take it this is -- this is March of 1995, correct? I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall seeing this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If -- if I can ask you, apart from this document did you have any data for the months up to March 1995 as to amounts of aid that were projected -- that were supposed to get through and amounts of aid that actually did get through to the enclaves when drafting your reports and reaching your conclusions that you testified about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, with respect to my reports the documents with respect to the convoys are issues I've testified. They aren't dealt with in my reports, we didn't have these documents early on and I certainly didn't look at them early on. And again, as I've testified, I've not done a broad statistical analysis with respect to how many convoys departed, how many arrived, and what percentage of them were either turned around or what percentage of cargo was taken off under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'd like to move to a different topic. The first day of direct examination and several times thereafter you focused on the inclusion of civilian population in certain VRS military orders and have testified about what you think that means. By way of refreshing everyone's memory, T -- transcript page 16141 is one such example in relation to P2095 and perhaps we can call up P2095 for purposes of the next few questions. Now, sir, in direct you focused on the language at item number 1 that says: "Launch on attack using the main body of troops and major equipment to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up or force them to surrender, and force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde." Now, if I'm correcting recalling your testimony you seemed to imply that while it was okay to direct an attack on the enemy soldiers and while you acknowledged the Bosnian Muslim soldiers withdrew their support for the civilian population, you implied that this order was illegitimate or demonstrated an attempt to violate international law because of the inclusion of the Muslim local population. Am I correctly understanding your evidence, and if not please correct me.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I recall that I said was that -- it was -- I didn't pass actually, I don't believe, a value judgement on that issue. What I believe I said was that it is inappropriate to target civilian population or objects, make them the target of a military attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ultimately the issue of lawfulness is a matter for the Court to decide, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at transcript page 16.143, lines 17 to 18, in answering Judge Orie's follow-up question you elaborate by saying: "It is a recognition in my particular case that something can have military utility yet still be patently unlawful." Does that fresh your recollection if you were --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was my comment back to Judge Orie and his question. From a legal perspective obviously it's contradictory that something could have military value or have a military utility as a tactic and yet be unlawful. The fact is that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you'll agree with me, I think, that there is a stark difference between a military temporarily removing a civilian population from a zone of combat on the one hand and a military permanently removing a population on the other hand, am I right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I would distinguish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that where a party is intended to engage in combat with an opposing force, the civilians usually leave the combat zone of their own accord as the fighting gets close to them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect the answer is that where possible civilians do not want to find themselves in the line of fire, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me based on your military background, experience, and expertise that the ABiH forces operating in this same area had an affirmative obligation under international military law to remove themselves from areas populated by civilians, so as to prevent the civilian population from becoming, in essence, a human shield exposed to potential combat?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, sir. My understanding is that all warring parties, to the degree that they can to take steps to ensure that they can conduct combat operations in a way that minimise the risk to civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the case of combat, either initiated by or foreseen by the ABiH forces, would you agree that the ABiH forces in this area had an affirmative obligation to move civilians from amongst the combat zone to areas of safety?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In abstract I would. In the context of what was actually happening, I guess the question that I would have is: Where would you move them to an area that the ABiH would be considered safe? I mean in this context again we are talking about a -- while rather large pocket, it is one that is behind the lines of VRS territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree that the ABiH forces in this area had an obligation not to locate their military structures, like headquarters, weapons depots, and troop formations near civilian areas?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking about November of 1992 or are we talking about July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the 1992 for the time-period of the document.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that the military forces of the ABiH that were operating in the Cerska or Udrc regions at the time had weapons depots and things of that nature. Certainly the military forces would be under an obligation to not set up military targets or, where possible, not use populated villages as a key component of their defence lines where they could. Again, it's a matter of practical aspect. I mean, if the village is in the middle of the road and you need to fight over the road, the village is going to become a military object at some juncture. Some things are not avoidable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, as to civilians that are caught in a combat zone, perhaps due to the ABiH's failures to live up to obligations, would you agree that the VRS has a legitimate incentive to engage in a tactic to attempt to modify the civilian-to-combatant ratio in that area so as to try to cure the ABiH's non-compliance and minimise collateral damage that would have been expected from legitimate combat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, that's long and confusing and it also assumes facts not in evidence. It would have to be done as a hypothetical, which I don't have a problem with a hypothetical --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is a hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, to some extent one of the seven questions certainly puts some hypothesis under it. But, Mr. Ivetic, could you please rephrase all of your seven questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and I could perhaps even cut them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When a party is contemplating combat, isn't it a legitimate tactic to attempt to modify the civilian-combatant ratio in that area so as to try to minimise collateral damage that would be expected from such legitimate combat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's still three questions in one, and apart from that it's all hypothetical. And of course a tactic -- whether a tactic is legitimate or not also depends, of course, which means are used in order to -- could you please be concrete, Mr. Ivetic, and put to the witness what apparently you want to suggest was the situation in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was the VRS entitled to engage in attempts to modify the civilian-combatant ratio in an area prior to engaging in combat to try to minimise collateral damage?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess what I am unclear about in your question is what you mean by the phrase "modify the civilian-combatant ratio."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Modify the non-combatant to combatant ratio, sir. It's a term of art in the military, I believe, for reducing the number of civilians in an area, so as to do your proportionality analysis to determine if a military action with a military purpose, even with a risk for collateral damage, is -- gets a green light or a go order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you -- if he's now defining this term of reducing the Muslims in an area --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I didn't say "Muslims" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- you said a reducing of the number of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Given how many civilians were forcibly transferred or murdered in this war, I think we should have a clear meaning of what he means by "reducing civilians."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Getting them out of the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means -- or would you leave that entirely open.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it's a hypothetical question, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey asked me to make a hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say take a balloon and put them all in a balloon and take them out, that might be different from loading them into buses and driving them out and that may be different. There are so many options, so therefore to say -- to ask whether this would be legitimate or not, let's try to stick to the facts as they were there rather than to lose ourselves in the abstract possibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just -- I was going to say what Judge Orie is saying. But I just want to look at this document that's on the screen which is the source of all of these questions that are hypothetical at this stage. Mr. Ivetic, what you read to the witness before you asked these questions is a passage that says: "Launch an attack using the main body of troops and major equipment to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up or force them to surrender, and force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde." Now, these are facts stated as not in hypotheses, just stating what should be done. I thought if you confine yourself to what is said here we would understand your questions better.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I realise that, Your Honour. Unfortunately, the problem we have is the English translation of this document is not true to the B/C/S which is what I was getting to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you ask for a better translation, but this does not -- is -- it's not an explanation on how you put your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. But I was under the impression that he was a military expert, not that he's been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I think the matter is clear to you now. Mr. McCloskey, anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just that we completely disagree on the interpretation issue, so you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is an interpretation issue which should be resolved, the Chamber is always assisting in getting the best translation, and finally the Chamber will have to interpret on the basis of the best available translation what the document tells us yes or no. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just one observation, this document is already in evidence and when it was tendered it was not objected in relation to the quality of the translation. It is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, if there's any serious translation problem, it would have been better to raise it, as suggested by Judge Fluegge, when it was admitted. But if there is any thing that came up later, then please don't hesitate to have it all verified, but don't use it as an excuse for the way in which you are phrasing your questions at this moment. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's go to very specific examples then. Sir, would you agree that in the case of this region during that specific time-period, it was not available to the VRS to drop warning leaflets to areas that were going to be subjected to combat due to the no-fly zone that was imposed on that region?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one explanation, I guess. I mean, I don't know from my reading of the military documents that -- and again, with respect to 1992, I mean other people have studied that in more depth than I have. I'm not aware that there was ever an intent to drop leaflets or documents and that the issue of whether or not there was a no-fly zone or not had any bearing on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute about the answer to this question, that a no-fly zone would have prevented throwing leaflets? Mr. McCloskey, I'm not asking you about the relevance of it; I'm asking you whether there's any dispute about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know. I just don't know. If the VRS had asked for a special request so they could act like the US army acted in Vietnam, whether that would have been approved or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't know. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If done correctly, don't modern military forces use a concept of warning shots before a ground attack against combatants in an area as a means to minimise the presence of civilians when ground troops go in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Ivetic. Again you are asking theory. You are not asking what happened. Were warning shots raised if they were -- warning shots were shot. Put it to the witness that they were shot at that time and let him say whether he knows or doesn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn to his report number 04627, page 36 in English, page 38 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for that, sir, I can tell you this is in relation to your Srebrenica narrative revised where you describe how the VRS forces were able to move the Dutch UNPROFOR without actually targeting them as such or creating injuries upon them. It starts at 3.15: "As the day wore on, the VRS forces continued to advance on Dutch blocking positions using fire and manoeuvre tactics to force them back without actually firing directly on Dutch troops. Thus, despite the intensity of the conflict, the Dutch did not suffer casualties as a result of VRS fire ..." Later on in this same paragraph you say: "Using the same tactics of fire and manoeuvre tactics, the VRS continued to force the Dutch back, until the blocking positions were in the town proper." Sir, would you agree with me that by not actually targeting the Dutch troops as such, the VRS had demonstrated an ability to effectively use fire and movement tactics to clear both combatants, non-combatants, and the DutchBat from an area without directly attacking them or causing unnecessary collateral damage?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. What I said is what I meant, that when firing in the direction of the Dutch Battalion, that is the tactic they employed. I have no information that suggests that that is the same tactic they employed when firing at Bosnian Muslim military units in July of 1995. I limited that observation to the Dutch Battalion for those particular days.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what about the civilians that would have been near the DutchBat according to the narrative and the evidence, would they also have been moved in the same manner without injuries?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, as evidenced in my narrative - and I don't believe that any additional information has come to the contrary, during the actual several-day operation where the VRS attacked down into and towards Srebrenica, I don't recall documents indicating that, you know, as they were heading towards Srebrenica that they would otherwise not distinguish between military and civilians. I don't recall them deliberately targeting civilians or being in a position to until potentially the 10th, when they were actually in a position to fire on the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can get back to P2095 now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you kindly pause between questions and answers for the interpreters. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can focus on the paragraph in question again, number 1. In English it says: "An attack," in the Serbian attack would be "napadati" which is not found in that paragraph. What is found are the words --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to object to any of his off-the-cuff translation issues. He's corrupting the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Should I read it in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, Mr. Ivetic, you know that our interpreters are not serving as translators. And therefore, a verification of the translation of a written document should be submitted to CLSS and that procedure should not be replaced by either you telling us what the words are and what they mean or to read them to the interpreters. And if there's any need on this specific matter to see whether the translation should be revised, the Chamber will try to assist you in order to have that urgently done. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this has clearly been a deliberate tactic to bring up translation issues to Mr. Butler at the last minute. This document is clearly something that has been planned for. Mr. Butler does like to consider things counsel says and takes it seriously. So I think by not objecting to this -- this or other related intercepts at this point he has waived his right to get into this issue. And certainly not to drop his new versions on things. Now we can discuss, as we do, afterward and if there are documents, as we have recently done, that we can work an agreement on as we can, I'm open to do that, but this is really -- this is a deliberate snaggle.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do I need to respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic -- well, that the way in which you introduced the translation issue was not the most elegant one --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I think you agree with that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I've been on my feet for eight hours. So, yes, I agree, Your Honours, I'm not exactly the most elegant at times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you have an opportunity after the court hearing to make any attempt to have the translation revised, and the request of the observation by Mr. McCloskey that you've waived your right is not adopted by the Chamber. And I would invite you to use better arguments than the one that you are eight hours on your feet. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with the concept known as an undefended or an open city as opposed to a defended city under the rubric of the Additional Protocols of the Geneva Convention and, more closely to home, US army doctrines as first established by field manual 27-10.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And by undefended city, will you agree with me that the definition requires an undefended place within the meaning of Article 25 HR or the Additional Protocols in the Geneva Convention, depending on which source one draws from, as being an inhabited place near or in a zone where opposing armed forces are in contact which is open for occupation by an adverse party without resistance. In order to be considered as undefended the following conditions should be fulfilled: Armed forces and all other combatants as well as mobile weapons and mobile military equipment must have been evacuated or otherwise neutralised; no hostile use should be made of fixed military installations or establishments; no acts of warfare shall be committed by the authorities or by the population; and no activities in support of military operations shall be undertaken. Do you agree with that definition, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of "undefended"? I don't know where -- what are we suggesting is undefended?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you inform the Chamber whether the relevance is found in Srebrenica to be an undefended city? Because then we could first ask the witness whether he considers that that was the case. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's the question I want to ask him whether he considers this area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- that was the subject of this order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, let's then try not to waste too much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first question is: Did you consider, with your knowledge of international law, Srebrenica to be an undefended city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've never defined it as an undefended city with respect to the protections that it was involved. Even though there's obviously a substantial civilian presence and a United Nations presence, my understanding of an open city is that a party has to declare it as such. And I'm unaware of the Bosnian Muslim political or military leadership making a declaration that Srebrenica is an open city. So in that respect, I've never considered it as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to this same area, would you define it as a defended city under the same international instruments?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you should give the witness some time to think about --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the answer because it is time to adjourn. I also put on the record that, Mr. Ivetic, you are now at approximately eight hours and 35 minutes at this moment. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom, but I again -- one second, Mr. Butler, one second. I would like to instruct you again not to speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, which will continue early next week because we'd like to see you back on Monday morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. But before I ask you to leave. Mr. McCloskey, could you give us an indication now after a major part of the cross-examination having -- is behind us, whether -- how much time you approximately need for re-examination in seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I've been thinking about that with the re-opening of directive 4, that opens up a big area, but I don't want to spend hours there so -- and I know that you don't either. So right now I see one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One session, which means that most likely we'll not conclude on Monday, but there's a fair chance that we would on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and we'll resume Monday, the 16th of September, 2013, at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 16th day of September, 2013, at 9.30 a.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.18 p.m.,
